title: Responder Proficiency Curriculum and Failover Catalog
author: Claire Chen
content:
Summary:
This document defines a structured proficiency curriculum for responders at Redwood Inference and a canonical failover catalog for common multi-service failure classes. It is intended to be a single reference for on-call onboarding, continuous assessment, and game-day scenarios. The curriculum focuses on recovery patterns (containment, mitigation, full failover) and communication templates for status pages and customer-facing notices.

Purpose:
- Reduce time-to-competence for new responders.
- Provide repeatable practice through scheduled game days and micro-simulations.
- Capture tested failover actions and ownership for quick reference during incidents.

Scope:
This page covers:
- Responder proficiency levels and learning objectives.
- A 6-month curriculum and suggested cadence.
- Failover catalog for 8 failure classes with immediate actions.
- Assessment rubric and certification criteria.
- Status page and customer comm templates (short, follow-up, resolved).
- Game-day recipes and scoring.

Audience:
- New on-call engineers, SREs, team leads, and incident commanders.
- Owners of services integrated with Redwood: serving runtime teams, API gateway, and SRE.

Learning objectives by proficiency level:
1) Observer (shadow, 0–2 weeks)
   - Understand the incident lifecycle and key tooling (PagerDuty, Slack bridge, Status page).
   - Read basic runbooks and recognize service ownership.
2) Responder (solo triage, 2–8 weeks)
   - Execute containment steps from runbooks with supervision.
   - Make clear customer-facing status updates using templates.
3) Operator (independent, 2–6 months)
   - Initiate failovers, rollback model versions, and manage hotfix releases.
   - Lead a bridge and coordinate multi-team escalations.
4) Incident Commander (IC, certified)
   - Orchestrate large incidents, prioritize business impact, and sign postmortems.

6-month curriculum (compact syllabus):
- Week 0: Orientation and tools (PagerDuty, Ops bridge, incident board).
- Week 1–2: Shadow shifts with Observer checklist (5 shadowed incidents).
- Week 3–4: Execute Responder checklist on low-severity incidents (with mentor).
- Month 2: Two micro-simulations (30–90 minute blameless drills).
- Month 3: Full-day game day focused on slow memory leak → degraded throughput.
- Month 4: Cross-team escalation tabletop for multi-region network partition.
- Month 5: Failover enactment day (promote standby region, validate routing).
- Month 6: IC assessment and written practical (runbook execution + status comms).

Assessment rubric (pass thresholds):
- Technical steps: 60% correctness (runbook actions executed in order).
- Communication: 80% clarity & timeliness (initial note within 15 minutes, updates every 30 minutes for SEV2+).
- Leadership: 70% coordination (escalations made appropriately, triage loop closed).
- Certification: pass two live incidents as primary responder + one formal game-day score >= 80.

Failover catalog (index of canonical mitigations)
Format: Failure class | Symptom | Immediate containment (first 15m) | Owner | Safe fallback
| Network partition - control plane | API 5xxs / spikes in error budget | Isolate cross-region traffic, route new traffic to healthy region via traffic manager; open bridge; engage networking SRE | eng-sre | Promote standby region, read-only degrade
| Model KV cache corruption | Incorrect tokenization / generation fuzzing | Quarantine model variant, evict KV cache, rollback to last-known-good model version | eng-serving-runtime | Route to CPU quantized fallback slot
| GPU OOM cascade | abrupt OOMs, node churn, queue pile-up | Scale down batch sizes, requeue work, cordon GPU node, drain workloads | gpu-fleet | Throttle new sessions; fall back to smaller model variant
| External datastore latency | elevated DB p99/tails | Enable local cache bypass TTL, reduce write volume, degrade non-critical features | eng-platform | Switch to read-replica, engage DB on-call
| Auth/Token service outage | token validation errors | Bypass non-critical token checks for partner-only traffic (pre-approved list), rotate keys after containment | security | Fail open for low-risk internal endpoints, otherwise reject
| Autoscaler thrash | oscillating scale events | Pause autoscaler, revert to fixed capacity, open stability incident, collect metrics | eng-sre | Return to last stable capacity config
| Config rollout regressions | sudden config-driven defects | Rollback config via controlled change set, enable feature flags to disable offender | product | Roll forward hotfix after testing in canary
| Cache stampede | cache melt-down, DB extra load | Apply probabilistic jitter, reduce cache TTLs progressively, increase cache pool | eng-platform | Put aggressive rate limits; serve stale while repairing cache

Immediate actions template (first 15 minutes)
1) Acknowledge (PagerDuty) + declare initial severity.
2) Open bridge and post incident card in #incident-ops with service, symptoms, and owner.
3) Short status to customers (see template A).
4) Run short diagnostics: p95 latency, p99 errors, capacity headroom, recent deploys.
5) Execute the catalog containment actions for the matched failure class.

Status page templates
- Template A — Initial Notice (short):
  "We are investigating increased errors for {service}. Scope: {regions affected}. Current impact: increased 5xx rate and elevated latency. Engineers are responding and we expect an update within 30 minutes. (Incident ID: {id})"

- Template B — Follow-up (30–60m):
  "Update: Mitigation steps underway. We have isolated the root cause to {component}. Traffic is being routed to healthy capacity in {regions}. Users may see intermittent errors for {subset of features}. ETA to recovery: {estimate}."

- Template C — Resolved + Next steps:
  "Resolved: The incident affecting {service} has been resolved at {time}. Root cause: {short summary}. Impact: {user-visible impact}. Actions taken: {rollback/patch/failover}. Next steps: {postmortem link + remediation owners}."

Customer comms (email / enterprise notice)
- Short enterprise template:
  Subject: [Redwood] Service disruption affecting {customer_product} — {time window}
  Body:
  "Hello {customer_contact},

  We experienced a service disruption impacting {scope} between {start} and {end}. Immediate mitigations: {actions}. Your data and requests were {safety statement}. We will share a detailed postmortem at {postmortem_link}. If you need priority support, reply to this email or open a customer ticket.

  — Redwood Inference Support"

Postmortem / blameless review template (to be attached to the incident card)
- Title: short summary + incident id
- Timeline: 5–15 minute resolution granularity for critical steps
- Impact: customers affected, request loss, throughput loss, SLO delta
- Root cause analysis: contributing factors (human / code / infra / config)
- Containment steps and time to containment
- Corrective actions with owners and due dates (P1/P2/P3)
- Follow-up validation plan and acceptance criteria

Game-day recipes and scoring
- Micro-sim (30m): Simulate increased p50 latency. Goals: exercise initial triage and status comms. Scoring: technical 30, comms 20, process 10.
- Medium sim (3h): Introduce cascading failures: KV cache then datastore tail-latency. Goals: practice failover catalog and cross-team escalations. Scoring: technical 40, comms 30, leadership 30.
- Mega-day (8h): Multi-region failover + customer comms. Includes surprise degraded SLA injection. Scoring: technical 50, comms 30, leadership 20.

Scoring rubric highlights:
- Technical correctness: were containment steps correct and safe? (0–50)
- Communication: clarity, cadence, customer empathy, and accuracy (0–30)
- Leadership: escalation, documentation, and decision-making (0–20)

Runbook hygiene checklist (owners must verify monthly)
- Steps numbered, with time-to-complete estimates.
- Clear roll-back instructions and safety checks.
- Contact list with primary and secondary on-call.
- Dependencies listed (datastores, 3rd party services).
- Test steps and a smoke test command.
- Last runbook execution date and last sign-off.

Operational artifacts to maintain alongside this curriculum
- Incident board template with fields: incident_id, start_time, severity, primary_owner, impact, current_action, next_update.
- Bridge recording policy: record high-severity incidents and store in incident archive for 12 months.
- Training log per responder: incidents participated, game-days scored, certifications earned.

Ownership and maintenance
- Document owner: Eng SRE curriculum lead (rotation: quarterly).
- Runbook owners: service teams (listed in each runbook header).
- Curriculum owner: Eng Developer Experience (training & assessments).

How to certify as IC (practical steps)
1) Complete the 6-month curriculum.
2) Lead at least two SEV2+ incidents as IC under mentorship.
3) Complete written practical (scenario + comms).
4) Obtain sign-off from two reviewers (SRE manager + product reliability lead).

Appendix: Quick commands and smoke checks
- Check serving health: curl -sS https://internal-api.{region}.redwood/healthz | jq .
- Queue depth: kubectl get hpa -n serving --output jsonpath='{.items[*].status.currentReplicas}'
- Clear model KV cache (example): curl -X POST https://internal-admin/kv/evict -d '{\"model\": \"m-1\"}'

Notes and change log:

If you are training a new responder, start with the Observer checklist and schedule the first micro-sim within week 2. For questions, ping #eng-oncall-curriculum or email eng-dx@redwood.com.
